HEADLINE: 'More cockroaches' at Slater & Gordon
INTRO: Exclusive | Sydney-based fund manager VGI Partners has warned there is "more than one cockroach in the kitchen" of Slater & Gordon, after the ASX-listed law firm revealed an accounting error and confirmed it was the subject of a regulatory probe.
TEXT:
Exclusive | Sydney-based fund manager VGI Partners has warned there is "more than one cockroach in the kitchen" of Slater & Gordon, after the ASX-listed law firm revealed an accounting error and confirmed it was the subject of a regulatory probe.

Slater & Gordon's share price plunged 25 per cent to $3.78 after it said the Australian Securities and Investments Commission had raised queries with the company and its auditors, Pitcher Partners. The company had initially denied a report by the The Australian Financial Review last week that revealed the corporate watchdog was holdings discussions with Pitcher Partners. Douglas Tynan, a partner at VGI, told the Financial Review that there was likely to "be more to come" from Slater & Gordon, and described the company's revelations of an error in the consolidation of the accounts of its recently acquired UK UK operation as "a highly unusual accounting error".

"The company now acknowledges that cash receipts from customers have been overstated,," VGI partner Douglas Tynan told the AFR. He said the errors went to the heart of the questions over the way Slater & Gordon recognised revenue.

HEADLINE: Grexit fears wipe $38b from ASX
SUBHEAD: Hockey moves to allay investor concerns
INTRO: The freezing of Greece's banks as it lurches towards bankruptcy, and huge losses in Chinese equities have unleashed the second-worst day for Australian stocks this year and set up an unsteady beginning to the new fiscal year for financial markets.
TEXT:
The freezing of Greece's banks as it lurches towards bankruptcy, and huge losses in Chinese equities have unleashed the second-worst day for Australian stocks this year and set up an unsteady beginning to the new fiscal year for financial markets.

"Market volatility's coming," warned Kumar Palghat, chief investment officer at Kapstream Capital, citing Greece's uncertain future in the eurozone, weakness in China's economy, stretched asset prices globally and whether these factors could stymie the United States' recovery. "Everybody that bought into the European Union always expected that every member would be a permanent member. Now the permanency of that union is coming into question," he said.

Greek banks will be shut for the rest of the week ahead of the July 5 referendum called by Greek Prime Minister Alexis Tsipras. The country is poised to miss its Tuesday deadline to repay €1.5 billion ($2.18 billion) to the International Monetary Fund without a credit lifeline.

Treasurer Joe Hockey, in Beijing to sign up Australia as a member of China's Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, sought to assure Australians that the growing risk of a Greece exit from the eurozone was sufficiently contained.

"The fundamental problem is that Greece has no willpower to undertake the reforms that are necessary to get themselves back on track," he told The Australian Financial Review. "When you compare that to Spain and Italy who have taken some reforms, you can see there is a strong contrast with what's happened and is happening in Greece and what has happened in other parts of Europe."

He described Australia's exposure to Greece is "very limited and quarantined," adding that the Reserve Bank of Australia and the prudential and securities regulators were communicating with Treasury on the situation.

Volatility in markets escalated when trading in China reopened, failing to lift on the back of a rate cut and further stimulatory action from the People's Bank of China over the weekend. Chinese stocks are firmly in a bear market after the Shanghai Composite fell 3.3 per cent, extending losses to 22 per cent from its peak. The Shenzhen-based, technology-focused ChiNext Composite is down 30 per cent from its June high following a 7.4 per cent loss on Monday. The Shanghai market had more than doubled in the past year and is now in a savage fear-fuelled sell-off.

In Australia, the S&P/ASX 200 Index shed 123 points to close at 5422.50 points, erasing 2.2 per cent, led by falls in the banking sector. The Australian dollar slipped to US76.43¢ and traders priced in a higher chance of an interest rate cut from the Reserve Bank coming dollar slipped to US76.43¢ and traders priced in a higher chance of an interest rate cut from the Reserve Bank coming later this year.

A brewing concern for the domestic economy is that Europe's Greece problem and the end of the bull market in China could give the United States Federal Reserve cause to delay a targeted lift in interest rates if the recovery slows. That would keep the value of the US dollar suppressed and leaves the Australian currency at levels the RBA deems overvalued, supporting the case for further easing.

Global fund manager and PM Capital founder Paul Moore, who visited Greece on a fact finding mission earlier this year but declined to invest because of the political risks, said that the economy's promise had been "smashed" by the leadership's fumbling of talks with creditors and the unwillingness among lenders to budge on some key measures.

"There were green shoots starting to appear," Mr Moore said. "Now, even if they recover, it's going to be from a much lower level again … If the patient is in intensive care, you don't ask him to do push-ups to make himself stronger."

His fund is sitting on the sidelines until there is some direction around Greece's place in the monetary union and what currency it emerges with. "If the stock prices were down 90 per cent then, I wouldn't care about what currency they're in, but they're not. Until we understand what we're dealing with, it's just a crapshoot."

Mr Moore said the bigger concern for Australian investors was China. "Look at the size of the Greek economy, it's a speck.

"China's not a speck."

Greek 10-year bond yields soared to the highest since 2012 and yields in other euro area periphery economies rose, pushing up the cost of borrowing. "There's a lot of problems out there and it just shows, six years into the US recovery, there's a lot of things that can derail it," ANZ senior interest rates strategist Martin Whetton said. On Sunday, Washington confirmed that US Treasury Secretary Jack Lew telephoned Mr Tsipras urging a resolution. He has made similar overtures to the IMF and European finance ministers.

"They're playing chicken and it's not likely to end well for Greece," Mr Whetton said. "The big risk is the EU walks away in complete frustration and lets them default."

The European Central Bank could have a greater role to play if yields keep rising as contagion spreads around Europe, by boosting bond purchases under its €1.1 trillion monetary stimulus program, which began in January.

But that still means that Greece and its creditors face an inevitable decision about dealing with its roughly €300 billion of outstanding debt. Because most of the debt has been absorbed from the private sector and into the hands of groups such as the IMF since the sovereign debt crisis, Greece will technically be in arrears and not full-scale default when it misses its June 30 payment.

"In the short term, I think markets are not good with political risk therefore they panic," AquAsia credit strategist Mark Bayley said, agreeing that China was a bigger concern.

As for Australia's bigger trade partner, "the direct economic linkages with China are much higher," Mr Warner cautioned.

HEADLINE: Get budgets in order, Hockey warns
INTRO: Treasurer Joe Hockey says the situation facing Greece was a wake-up call for countries which do not get their budgets under control.
TEXT:
Treasurer Joe Hockey says the situation facing Greece was a wake-up call for countries which do not get their budgets under control.

Mr Hockey said Australia was "well placed" for a Greek exit.

"Treasury has been engaging with the Reserve Bank, Australian Prudential Regulation Authority and Australian Securities and Investments Commission and we are monitoring the situation closely," he said.

"This is a lesson for everyone. If you don't get your budget in shape when you can, the pain is always far greater later."

Mr Hockey who is in China to sign up Australia to the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank told reporters he would be discussing the Greek situation with other finance ministers.

"Australia's exposure to Greece is very limited and quarantined. There were strong messages from all of the Europeans I spoke to today to affirm that the Europeans have matters under control.

The Europeans are sending very strong messages of reassurance. Obviously, they are managing the process.

"There have been numerous countries that have defaulted on their IMF loans. The fundamental problem is that Greece has no willpower to undertake the reforms that are necessary to get themselves back on track. When you compare that to Spain and Italy who have taken some reforms, you can see there is a strong contrast with what's happened and is happening in Greece and what has happened in other parts of Europe. Australian markets should not overreact to the news from Europe because our exposure is very limited and Europeans have the matters well in hand."

HEADLINE: Eurozone likely to be stronger after referendum
INTRO: Global traders are up in arms that Greece, a country with only 11 million residents and annual GDP less than that of Israel or Chile, is giving them yet another bout of whip-lash.
TEXT:
Global traders are up in arms that Greece, a country with only 11 million residents and annual GDP less than that of Israel or Chile, is giving them yet another bout of whip-lash.

While there is deep anxiety as to how this chaotic Greek drama plays out, there may be counter-intuitive grounds for optimism.

First, there's a very good chance that the July 5 referendum called by the Greek Prime Minister, Alexis Tsipras, will break the intractable stalemate that has prevented politicians across Europe concluding their agonising, multi-month negotiations over extending the Greek bail-out.

Second, the decision to close Greece's banks and its stockmarket prior to the poll ensures there will be no disastrous bank run or Armageddon-like correction in local equities, although we can expect rising community discontent as the Greek main-street discovers the real-world consequences of trading insolvent.

Third, the unprecedented crisis coordination between the eurozone's political leaders, finance ministries, and regulatory agencies, combined with the prospect of Greece voting to formally accept the bail-out terms, should make the eurozone stronger in the long-run.

In particular, by financing Greece during a depression and accepting only partial repayment of this money, the eurozone is implementing a form of de facto "fiscalisation" that transfers wealth from richer countries to members in need and complements the conduct of its monetary policy.

Let's take a step back and consider the strategic rationale for the referendum and its potential consequences.

Tsipras was elected in January on an untenable platform of keeping Greece in the eurozone while rejecting fundamental reforms that were essential conditions for its "troika" of creditors, which include the European Central Bank (ECB), the European Commission (EC), and the International Monetary Fund (IMF). (In contrast to the first Greek drama in 2012, this one thankfully does not directly involve private banks.)

Tsipras's negotiating position has been complicated by the fact that significant communist power-blocks within his left-wing coalition want Greece to exit the eurozone and return to the Drachma in conflict with the desires of the Greek electorate, most of whom want to remain in the currency union. There is little popular appetite for becoming part of Vladimir Putin's poor kleptocracy.

While Greece's creditors were willing to make significant concessions, including eventual debt relief and further extending maturities on Greece's liabilities, the troika have been insistent on ensuring Greece engages in real policy reforms to its intellectually bankrupt tax, pension and public service systems, which have exacerbated its current malaise.

If Tsipras had rolled on the troika's demands over the weekend, he risked dissolving his own coalition, breaking promises made to the electorate only months ago, and ceding his role as prime minister. By shifting the burden of decision-making to the electorate, Tsipras is both empowering his people to divine their own destiny and - perhaps temporarily - protecting his political mandate by not doing anything that contradicts the people's preferences.

Tsipras is intimately familiar with public and private polling that implies Greece will vote in favour of accepting the troika's terms to stay in the eurozone.

The formulation of a yes/no response to a highly technical question on the troika's proposal will inevitably be translated by main-street into a call on eurozone membership.

This interpretation will be encouraged by politicians across the continent and an increasingly hostile Greek media as we move closer to the referendum. On the weekend Greece's Minister for Finance, Yanis Varoufakis, immediately conceded the country would probably vote "yes".

Despite highly critical rhetoric from the Greek government on the troika's bail-out terms, a poll in mid June found that 70 per cent of Greeks wanted to stay in the eurozone "at any cost".

On Sunday two new Greek polls were released that asked voters if they were in favour of accepting the troika's proposal. In the first, 57 per cent supported doing a deal (only 29 per cent opposed). And the second, which subjectively described the agreement as "painful", found only 33 per cent wanted to reject it.

Significantly, these polls were before the government had closed banks and ATMs, which will sharpen local concerns about the risks of leaving the eurozone.

Accounts from experts on the ground in Greece indicate the government expected the troika to accept its request for a one week extension to the negotiations, which was rejected, and the ECB to expand its emergency liquidity facilities to allow Greek banks to remain open, which it has not done.

HEADLINE: Cabcharge to allow for rivals
INTRO: Cabcharge's rivals could supplant its terminals in taxis after the competition watchdog on Monday forced the taxi payment network to allow competitors to process its cards after years of complaints it has frustrated access.
TEXT:
Cabcharge's rivals could supplant its terminals in taxis after the competition watchdog on Monday forced the taxi payment network to allow competitors to process its cards after years of complaints it has frustrated access.

After a report in The Australian Financial Review's Street Talk on Monday morning, the ACCC confirmed it had accepted an enforceable undertaking from Cabcharge to allow rival payment processors to process Cabcharge cards on their own taxi payment terminals.

Cabcharge shares fell 3.12 per cent to $3.72 on Monday.

"The undertaking opens up this market to further competition and will provide third parties with the ability to process Cabcharge cards for the first time," ACCC Chairman Rod Sims said.

Cabcharge cards are mainly used by businesses. Direct customers of Cabcharge accounted for $392 million of its $1.1 billion turnover in 2014. Competitors that have lost revenue since taxi payments levies were slashed in Victoria, NSW and Western Australia said the ACCC decision would give them the chance to earn more revenue and remain competitive.

HEADLINE: Slater & Gordon: between the lines
INTRO: The question for bewildered shareholders of Slater and Gordon - the once high-flying legal eagle - is whether there is more to come. If the analysis of VGI Partners, a Sydney-based fund manager that is shorting Slaters, is to be believed there "are more cockroaches in the kitchen" beyond the accounting error it revealed on Monday.
TEXT:
The question for bewildered shareholders of Slater and Gordon - the once high-flying legal eagle - is whether there is more to come. If the analysis of VGI Partners, a Sydney-based fund manager that is shorting Slaters, is to be believed there "are more cockroaches in the kitchen" beyond the accounting error it revealed on Monday.

In a detailed presentation obtained by The Australian Financial Review, the fund manager marched through several red flags it identified with the ASX-listed law firm's accounts. This led them to conclude that the 40-odd acquisitions undertaken by Slaters, including the recent $1.3 billion purchase of UK group Quindell, were more about buying legal work to disguise poor organic growth than expanding its empire.

At their core the issues around Slater and Gordon can be distilled into a simple question - when is a dollar a dollar? Law firms such as Slater and Gordon that conduct no-win no-fee business book revenues before they've been invoiced through what is known as Work in Progress (WIP) accounting. The more work the company takes on, the more its profits grow and by acquiring new law firms it's able to buy more work. If that work in undervalued at the time of the deal, it can revalue it upwards to grow earnings - or so the theory goes.

The pitfall of such a strategy is that while earnings are growing, the cash isn't coming through the door and the more acquisitions are made, the more funds must be raised from lenders and the sharemarket. Eventually, financing capacity is reached and the company faces a stress point.

What has concerned VGI is that the WIP balance has ballooned, nearly tripling in three years from $300 million to almost $1 billion, outpacing Slater and Gordon's revenue growth. At the same time, other balance sheet items such as accounts receivable and payable have surged. In sum, while Slater and Gordon may be showing spectacular growth in accounting profits, its cash position has gone the other way.

This might seem like it has nothing to do with an "arithmetic error" in the cash flow statements revealed to the ASX on Monday. The company confessed that it had found overstatements in the tens of millions in both its cash receipts and cash payments - the result of double counting tax and incorrect client disbursements - which had a neutral impact on the net cash balance. But there could very well be a link between cash flow discrepancies and WIP accounting.

A higher cash receipts balance would have the effect of overstating the extent to which Slater is converting both WIP and receivables into dollars. VGI has suggested as much. To neutralise this impact on the net cash position, cash payments would need to be inflated by the same amount, the presentation suggested. This would add weight to a theory that the errors revealed by the company on Monday, may reflect more than bad arithmetic and sloppy accounting. That will be one of several questions that will be posed to the company as it prepares to front investors, defend its accounting policies under queries from regulators and a faces up to a confrontation with hedge funds rarely seen in Australian finance.

For now Slater and Gordon is silent, "respecting a process" that is underway. History may not be on the ambitious law firm's side.

Australia's financial landscape is littered with roll-ups gone wrong, particularly professional services firms that have made profits by booking accounting gains rather than actual cash through the door.

HEADLINE: Australian deal activity tipped to reach next peak in 2018
INTRO: Australia will see its next peak in merger and acquisition activity in 2018, a year after global deals hit a similar high but a landmark report has predicted that deal activity won't hit the "bubble-like" heights seen prior to the global financial crisis.
TEXT:
Australia will see its next peak in merger and acquisition activity in 2018, a year after global deals hit a similar high but a landmark report has predicted that deal activity won't hit the "bubble-like" heights seen prior to the global financial crisis.

Law firm Baker & McKenzie commissioned Oxford Economics to undertake one of few quantitative assessments of the global deal landscape that also predicts activity across completed mergers and acquisitions (M&A) and initial public offerings (IPOs) through until the end of 2020. The report uses modelling techniques relating to historic changes in transaction flows and draws on structural and cyclical transaction drivers including national income growth, equity prices and interest rates.

Forecasts in the report have Australia's M&A annual completed deal value, including domestic and inbound transactions, edging up to $US74.1 billion ($96.1 billion) in 2015 from $US73.7 billion a year earlier. Activity is estimated to peak at $US126.3 billion in 2018, before slowing in the next two years.

Local Baker & McKenzie partner David Holland said while an uptick in global deal activity bodes well for increased transactions in Australia he noted a distinction between domestic and international trends.

"With regard to privatisations, we are back into the zone now with a bit more transaction activity," he told Fairfax Media, referring to state and federal government asset sales, many of which are under way. Mr Holland also noted that domestically the financial services sector, technology and telecommunications, the food and agribusiness industries and real estate were busy areas for dealmaking.

Globally, the report predicted the healthcare sector would continue to see rising M&A in the next three years while industries to watch included energy, consumer and technology, and telecoms. The analysis said completed global M&A activity would rise to $US2.7 trillion in 2015 and peak at $US3.4 trillion in 2017, before easing in the following three years.

"We do not expect the transaction peaks in 2017 and 2018 to be as high as those before the global financial crisis, as we are not experiencing the same bubble-like conditions prior to 2007," the report said. "As the global economic recovery continues, we expect central banks to begin raising interest rates in developed markets and equity markets to moderately decline."

Mr Holland echoed that view. "Broadly speaking a corporate could complete a piece of M&A right now and not feel like they are buying at the top of the market," he said. He also noted the untapped potential for Australian companies to pursue transactions in India and south-east Asia.

The analysis is based on global economic activity increasing to an average growth rate of 2.9 per cent per year over the next three years.

The report outlined risks to deal activity including events such as Greece exiting the eurozone, the UK leaving the European Union, a sharp fall in Chinese investment and the US raising interest rates faster than expected.

Australia failed to make the top 10 markets ranked by M&A or IPO activity growth in the five years to the end of 2020. For M&A, China led the pack with estimated growth of 153 per cent over the period, followed by Hong Kong and The Netherlands. In IPO markets, Egypt was tipped to have the strongest growth, followed by Spain and Vietnam.

Australia did, however, rank equal 10th with the US and Japan in a measure of a country's relative attractiveness as a destination for M&A and sharemarket listings.

The report predicted Australian IPO issuance would to fall to $US2.4 billion ($3.1 billion) this year, following record volumes in 2014. IPO volumes are then tipped to recover to $US6.6 billion in 2018.

But the report has its sceptics including UBS Australia's co-head of advisory Kelvin Barry. "I don't think you can accurately predict what is going to happen several years out as that is a function of many factors," he said.

Announced Australian targeted M&A, including domestic and inbound deals, have slipped 6 per cent year-to-date to $US45.8 billion in 2015 compared to last year, according to Dealogic. That is despite strong domestic and outbound transaction levels.

In the local M&A league tables, UBS sits in first spot working on deals worth $US22 billion. It is a whisker ahead of Macquarie Capital and Grant Samuel ranks third.

Bankers are confident M&A activity levels will hold up in the latter half of 2015.

"We see it [M&A] continuing but boards are sensibly cautious about undertaking M&A," Mr Barry said. "The capital and funding is there [for companies and private equity]."

Macquarie Capital's local chief executive Robin Bishop said M&A levels had been "reasonably solid" and noted the factors driving activity in 2015 remained in place including globalisation, industry consolidation and supportive funding markets across equity and debt.

A depreciating Australian dollar would likely also contribute to sustaining activity levels this year, Mr Bishop added, cautioning that business confidence remained "somewhat subdued".
